questions.stem: The principle of utmost good faith requires the proposer to:

opts.x: Disclose only the facts specifically asked about in the proposal form.
Disclose all facts material to the risk whether asked for or not.
Disclose only facts that are in the public domain.
Disclose only facts that have caused a loss in the previous five years.

questions.answer: (B) Disclose all facts material to the risk whether asked for or not.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The duty of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei), established in Carter v Boehm (1766) and confirmed repeatedly in Nigerian courts (Leadway Assurance v Zeco [2004]), requires the proposer to volunteer all information a prudent insurer would consider material in assessing the risk, even if the proposal form does not specifically ask for it. The duty is proactive and extends beyond answering the questions posed.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) is the ‘specific questions only’ position, it fundamentally underestimates the scope of the disclosure duty. An insured who answers all specific questions truthfully but omits a material fact not asked about has still breached utmost good faith.

(C) is incorrect; the test for materiality is what a prudent insurer would consider important, not whether the information is publicly available. Many material facts (a medical diagnosis, a criminal conviction) are not public.

(D) is incorrect; there is no five-year historical loss limitation on the disclosure obligation. A health condition from twelve years ago may still be highly material to a life insurance application.

questions.stem: Insurable interest in a life assurance policy taken on one’s own life:

opts.x: Is limited to the financial loss that would arise from the insured’s death.
Must be re-proved at the time of each claim.
Is unlimited in amount and need only exist at the time of contracting.
Requires a third party to confirm the financial relationship.

questions.answer: (C) Is unlimited in amount and need only exist at the time of contracting.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

A person has an unlimited insurable interest in their own life. The law presumes this without any requirement to quantify it. Insurable interest in a life policy need only exist at the time of contracting, not at the date of claim (unlike most indemnity policies). Once the policy is validly formed, its continuity does not depend on re-establishing interest.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) applies the creditor-debtor rule: a creditor’s interest in a debtor’s life is limited to the outstanding debt. This rule does not apply to a person’s own life, where interest is unlimited.

(B) is false, re-proving insurable interest at the date of claim is a rule for indemnity insurance (property insurance), where the insured must demonstrate they still own the insured property at the date of loss. Life assurance does not require this.

(D) has no basis in law. No third-party confirmation is required for a person’s interest in their own life.

questions.stem: The principle of indemnity is MOST accurately described as:

opts.x: The right of the insured to be paid the full sum insured regardless of actual loss.
The obligation to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, no more and no less.
A requirement that the insurer must always accept all claims presented.
A guarantee that the insured will profit from an insurance policy.

questions.answer: (B) The obligation to restore the insured to the same financial position as before the loss, no more and no less.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

Indemnity means making the insured whole, precisely compensating the actual financial loss suffered, no more and no less. The insured must not be better off after a loss than before it (which would create moral hazard, an incentive to generate insured events). The insured must not be worse off either (which would defeat the purpose of insurance). The principle is stated in Castellain v Preston (1883): ‘The contract of insurance... is a contract of indemnity, and... the indemnity means that [the insured] shall be fully indemnified, but shall never be more than fully indemnified.’
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) contradicts indemnity; the sum insured is the maximum payable but not the guaranteed amount. Payment is limited to actual loss, which may be below the sum insured.

(C) is incorrect; the insurer has the right to apply exclusions, conditions, and policy defences. Indemnity governs the measure of payment, not the right to refuse.

(D) is the opposite of indemnity. The principle expressly prohibits profit from insurance. An insured who profits from an insurance claim has over-recovered and the insurer’s subrogation rights will operate to recover the excess.

questions.stem: Which ONE of the following is a CORRECT statement about subrogation?

opts.x: Subrogation applies to life assurance policies.
The insurer may subrogate before paying the claim.
The insurer can recover from the third party only up to the amount it has paid as indemnity.
Subrogation gives the insurer the right to take over the insured’s entire business.

questions.answer: (C) The insurer can recover from the third party only up to the amount it has paid as indemnity.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Subrogation prevents unjust enrichment of both the insurer and the insured. The insurer steps into the insured’s shoes to pursue the party responsible for the loss, but its recovery is capped at the amount it paid in indemnity. If the insurer paid ₦8 million in settlement of a ₦10 million claim, it can recover at most ₦8 million from the tortfeasor. Any recovery above the amount paid goes to the insured to cover any shortfall (Yorkshire Insurance v Nisbet Shipping [1962]).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) is false, subrogation is a corollary of indemnity. Because life assurance is a contract of financial provision (not indemnity), subrogation does not arise. A life insurer that pays a death benefit cannot sue the party responsible for the death to recover the sum paid.

(B) reverses the correct sequence, subrogation can only arise after the insurer has fulfilled its obligation by paying the claim. It is not available as a pre-payment remedy.

(D) exaggerates the right entirely. Subrogation is a specific right to recover the particular loss for which indemnity was paid, not a general transfer of the insured’s commercial interests.

questions.stem: A warranty in an insurance contract:

opts.x: Can be breached without any consequence if the breach is minor.
Automatically discharges the insurer from liability on breach, regardless of any causal link to the loss.
Is a term that the insurer must satisfy before the policyholder can make a claim.
Is equivalent to a condition subsequent in its legal effect.

questions.answer: (B) Automatically discharges the insurer from liability on breach, regardless of any causal link to the loss.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A warranty is a fundamental term of the insurance contract at common law. Any breach, however minor and however unrelated to the eventual loss, discharges the insurer from further liability from the date of breach. This is the strict common law position confirmed in Bank of Nova Scotia v Hellenic Mutual [1992] and applied in Nigerian courts. An insured who warrants their vessel will not sail beyond certain waters, and then briefly exceeds those limits before returning, and later suffers a fire at port, may find the insurer discharged by the warranty breach, even though the breach had no connection to the fire.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) is false; there is no de minimis exception to warranty breach at common law. Even a trivial breach technically discharges the insurer.

(C) inverts the position. Warranties are obligations of the insured, not of the insurer. The insured warrants the truth of certain statements or undertakes to do (or not do) certain things.

(D) is incorrect. A condition subsequent terminates rights arising from a future event; a warranty breach has immediate effect from the moment of breach and is categorically different in its legal mechanism and consequence.

questions.stem:
Nnamdi applies for a life insurance policy. On the proposal form he answers 'No' to a question asking whether he has been diagnosed with any serious illness in the last five years. In fact, Nnamdi had been treated for hypertension eighteen months earlier but had forgotten about it. Nnamdi dies two years after the policy is incepted. The insurer discovers the undisclosed hypertension treatment and seeks to void the policy.
(a) Under the pre-NIIRA 2025 common law position, advise the insurer as to its right to avoid the policy, citing relevant Nigerian case authority.
(b) Explain how NIIRA 2025 modifies the analysis, and what remedy would be proportionate in these circumstances.

model.h: Part (a): Common Law Position

To void the policy for non-disclosure, the insurer must establish three elements: (i) materiality, would a prudent insurer consider the fact material in assessing the risk? (ii) non-disclosure or misrepresentation, did the insured fail to disclose the material fact? (iii) inducement, was the insurer induced to enter the contract by the non-disclosure?

(i) Materiality: Treated hypertension is unquestionably material. A life insurer assessing a standard life application would significantly elevate the risk assessment if it knew the applicant was being treated for cardiovascular hypertension. Nigerian courts have consistently applied the objective prudent insurer test: Adesanya v Royal Exchange (1986) CA; African Continental Bank v Nigerian General Insurance (1997) CA.

(ii) Non-disclosure: Nnamdi answered ‘No’ to a direct health question. This is both a failure to disclose and an affirmative misrepresentation.

(iii) Inducement: The insurer would not have accepted the risk at standard terms (or at all) had it known of the hypertension. This is a readily inferable presumption.

Under common law, the insurer’s right to void ab initio is established. The policy is voidable; if avoided, it is treated as never having existed and the insurer may return premiums but need pay no death benefit. The fact that the non-disclosure was innocent (Nnamdi genuinely forgot) is relevant to moral sympathy but not to legal entitlement under strict common law.
Part (b): NIIRA 2025 Modification

NIIRA 2025 introduced a proportionality framework requiring the insurer to consider what it would have done had the material information been disclosed, before selecting its remedy:

Route 1: Outright decline: If the insurer would have declined the proposal entirely (e.g., because severe uncontrolled hypertension was an absolute decline risk), avoidance of the policy and refusal of the claim remains available.

Route 2: Loaded premium: If the insurer would have accepted the risk but at a higher premium to reflect the elevated mortality, the proportionate remedy is to reduce the claim payout in proportion to the premium that should have been charged. E.g., if the standard premium was ₦180,000 and the loaded premium would have been ₦240,000, the claim is reduced to (₦180,000 / ₦240,000) = 75% of the sum assured.

Route 3: Exclusion: If the insurer would have accepted at standard premium with a cardiovascular exclusion, the hypertension-related death is excluded but other causes of death remain covered.

Applied to Nnamdi: Given that the hypertension was controlled (discovered in treatment) and he lived for 2 years post-inception, suggesting manageable risk, outright avoidance is likely disproportionate under NIIRA 2025. A loaded premium reduction applied to the claim is the most proportionate remedy. If the insurer cannot demonstrate it would have declined outright, NIIRA 2025 prevents it from using non-disclosure as a complete defence.

questions.stem: Explain the doctrine of proximate cause with reference to the decision in Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union [1918]. Apply the doctrine to the following scenario: an insured warehouse is damaged by flood, and during the flooding, thieves enter and steal goods. The fire and special perils policy covers flood but excludes theft. The insured claims for both flood damage and theft. Advise the insurer.

model.h: The Doctrine of Proximate Cause

The proximate cause doctrine holds that the insured event must be the proximate (dominant, effective, and real) cause of the loss, not merely the first event in a chain or the most recent event before the loss. Identifying the proximate cause cuts through the factual sequence to identify the root cause that set the chain in motion.

Leyland Shipping Co Ltd v Norwich Union [1918] AC 350: The Leyland vessel was torpedoed in World War I (a wartime exclusion). It was towed to a harbour of refuge at Le Havre, where it was grounded at a safe berth. Tidal action over several days caused it to sink. The insurer argued the proximate cause was the grounding at Le Havre (not an excluded event). The House of Lords held that the torpedo was the proximate cause throughout; it set the irreversible chain in motion. The tidal sinking was a manifestation of the torpedo’s original injury, not an independent new cause.
Application to the Warehouse Scenario

Flood causes structural damage to the warehouse, covered. During the flooding, thieves enter and steal goods, excluded.

The proximate cause analysis must determine whether the theft has the flood as its proximate cause (which would make it potentially covered as a consequence of a covered peril), or whether theft has an independent proximate cause breaking the chain from flood.

The critical distinction from Leyland: In Leyland, the torpedo directly and irreversibly caused the eventual sinking. In this scenario, the flood did not cause the theft. The flood created an opportunity that the thieves chose to exploit, but their criminal decision was an independent intervening act (novus actus interveniens). Absent the thieves’ independent decision to steal, no goods would have been stolen regardless of the flood.

Advice to insurer: The flood damage to the warehouse structure and any stock damaged by water is recoverable as a covered peril. The theft is not recoverable: theft is the proximate cause of the stolen goods’ loss, and theft is excluded. The flood was merely the background condition (not the proximate cause) of the theft. The insurer should meet the flood portion and decline the theft portion.

questions.stem: Distinguish between a warranty and a condition precedent in an insurance contract. Explain the legal consequences of breach of each, and discuss whether NIIRA 2025 modifies the traditional strict approach to breach of warranty in Nigerian insurance law.

model.h: Warranties: Definition and Consequences of Breach

A warranty is a fundamental term of the insurance contract, breach of which automatically discharges the insurer from all further liability, regardless of any causal connection between the breach and the loss. The insured may have warranted: the truth of a statement at inception (affirmative warranty); or a course of future conduct (promissory warranty). At common law, even a minor technical breach, entirely unrelated to the eventual loss, discharges the insurer. The insurer need not prove the breach contributed to the claim.
Conditions Precedent: Definition and Consequences of Breach

A condition precedent is a condition that must be fulfilled before a specific contractual right arises. In insurance, conditions precedent to the right to claim require the insured to take specific steps (e.g., notify the insurer within a defined period; provide documents; co-operate with investigations) before the claim becomes enforceable. Breach prevents the specific right from arising but does not, of itself, discharge the insurer from all future liability under the policy.

Key distinction: A warranty breach affects the entire contract from the date of breach. A condition precedent breach affects the specific claim to which the condition attaches, the policy continues for future claims.
NIIRA 2025 Modification

NIIRA 2025 introduced two significant modifications affecting warranty and condition precedent law:

1. For warranties, the proportionality framework (discussed in Q6) applies where the warranty relates to a misrepresentation or non-disclosure at inception. The insurer can no longer automatically void ab initio for any non-disclosure; it must consider proportionate remedies.

2. For conditions precedent (particularly notification clauses), NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection framework requires that conditions precedent to claims be clearly disclosed in plain language. Moreover, the prejudice test from NEM Insurance v Aderibigbe (2011 CA) (that mere delay in notification is insufficient to bar a claim without demonstrated prejudice to the insurer) is consistent with NIIRA 2025’s TCF obligation.

Conclusion: NIIRA 2025 softens the harsh edges of the traditional warranty doctrine for consumer life policies, without abolishing it. The strict automatic discharge position remains available where the insurer can demonstrate outright avoidance is proportionate to the breach.

questions.stem: Critically evaluate the doctrine of utmost good faith as applied in Nigerian insurance law prior to NIIRA 2025, with particular reference to the decisions in Leadway Assurance Co Ltd v Zeco Nigeria Ltd (2004) and NICON v Power & Industrial Engineering Co Ltd (1986). Assess the extent to which NIIRA 2025 achieves a fair balance between insurer security and policyholder protection.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

The pre-NIIRA 2025 doctrine of utmost good faith in Nigerian insurance law was robust in its theoretical foundation but disproportionate and commercially damaging in its primary remedy: automatic avoidance for any material non-disclosure, regardless of the insured’s good faith, the severity of the breach, or its connection to the claimed loss. NIIRA 2025 represents a genuine improvement through proportionality, but falls short of the standard set by the UK Insurance Act 2015.
Analysis of the Leading Cases

Leadway Assurance Co Ltd v Zeco Nigeria Ltd (2004) 11 NWLR (Pt 884) 316 (SC): The Supreme Court confirmed that an insurer may void a policy for material misrepresentation in the proposal form even if the non-disclosed fact had no causal connection to the eventual loss. The insured’s failure to disclose a prior claim history on a cargo policy entitled the insurer to avoid, regardless of whether the new claim involved the same risk.

Critical evaluation: The Leadway decision gave insurers a powerful, disproportionate avoidance weapon. An insured who innocently forgot a minor prior claim could find the entire policy avoided, a result that the court acknowledged was harsh but felt constrained to apply by the strict common law position.

NICON v Power & Industrial Engineering Co Ltd (1986) 1 NWLR (Pt 20) 1 (SC): Established that the materiality test is objective, what a prudent insurer would consider material, not subjective (what the insured thought was relevant). The insured’s honest belief that information was immaterial affords no protection if a prudent insurer would have wanted to know it.

Critical evaluation: The objective test is commercially necessary, insurers cannot manage risk on information they do not have. But it creates an asymmetry: policyholders, often without legal or insurance expertise, cannot always know what a ‘prudent insurer’ considers material. This information asymmetry favours insurers.
NIIRA 2025 Assessment

NIIRA 2025’s proportionality framework (applying the ‘what would we have done?’ test before selecting a remedy) is a genuine improvement. It prevents opportunistic avoidance of policies where the non-disclosure was innocent and the insurer would have accepted the risk at a higher price.

Shortcomings:
• NIIRA 2025 does not go as far as the UK Insurance Act 2015, which abolished automatic avoidance for consumer policies entirely.
• No statutory ‘reasonable search’ standard: the insured’s duty to disclose remains unbounded in scope; NIIRA 2025 does not tell policyholders clearly what they must disclose.
• No independent insurance ombudsman: disputes about proportionality remain in NAICOM’s Consumer Protection Bureau or the courts, both of which are resource-intensive for individual policyholders.

Conclusion: NIIRA 2025 moves the balance materially toward fairness. It is not perfect. The next legislative iteration should consider fully importing the UK Insurance Act 2015 consumer insurance model.

questions.stem: 'The principle of indemnity and the doctrine of subrogation are conceptually inseparable.' Discuss this proposition, explaining how each principle reinforces the other, and evaluate the practical challenges of enforcing subrogation rights in the Nigerian insurance market.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

Indemnity and subrogation are not merely related but are logically interdependent. Subrogation is the mechanism that gives effect to indemnity where a third party is responsible for the loss. Without indemnity, subrogation has no purpose; without subrogation in applicable cases, indemnity would be routinely breached by double recovery.
The Conceptual Link

Indemnity prohibits profit from insurance: the insured must not receive more than their actual financial loss. Where a third party caused the loss, the insured could potentially recover twice: once from the insurer (under the policy) and once from the tortfeasor (in the courts). Double recovery constitutes profit from misfortune, which violates indemnity.

Subrogation prevents this: once the insurer has paid the claim, it acquires the insured’s rights against the responsible third party. The insured is fully restored (indemnity satisfied). The insurer recovers from the party who caused the loss (the economic burden of the loss falls on its originator). The insured cannot pursue the tortfeasor independently; their interest has been extinguished by the insurance payment.

Castellain v Preston (1883): ‘The contract of insurance... is a contract of indemnity... The assured shall not recover more than a full indemnity. If... the same party should chance to recover damages... the insurer is entitled to have recourse to this.'

Practical illustration: Insured’s vehicle is written off in an accident caused by a third party’s negligence. Insurer pays ₦15m as the agreed market value. The insurer is subrogated to the insured’s right to sue the negligent third party and, if successful, recovers up to ₦15m. The insured cannot also sue the third party for the same loss (Yorkshire Insurance v Nisbet [1962]).
Practical Challenges of Subrogation in Nigeria

1. Tortfeasor insolvency: A very significant proportion of Nigerian motor accident tortfeasors have no assets and no motor insurance (despite TPMI being compulsory). The right of subrogation exists in theory; recovery in practice is often nil.

2. Legal process cost and delay: Subrogation actions require litigation. Nigeria’s court system, while improving, is not known for swift resolution of commercial disputes. Many subrogation actions cost more to pursue than they recover.

3. Fraudulent collusion: Where the insured and the tortfeasor are connected (family members, business partners), the subrogation action may face a non-cooperative defendant.

4. Statutory limitations: Certain third-party claims in Nigeria are subject to short limitation periods that may expire before the insurer’s subrogation right is exercised.

Conclusion: The conceptual inseparability of indemnity and subrogation is valid and principled. Nigerian insurers should assess recovery prospects realistically before committing litigation resources, and should consider whether aggregating subrogation recoveries into a specialist recovery unit (rather than managing them case-by-case) would improve the economics of recovery.
